A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same multilingual image-caption study. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial retitling and reorganization.

before.justification: v3 reports original caption analyses, GIT fine-tuning experiments, translation evaluations and an English/Japanese human captioning study.

after.justification: v4 retains these original empirical results and adds an evaluation using multilingual embeddings without translation.

M1.justification: The underlying translation, scene-graph extraction and canonicalization, coverage measurements, and GIT fine-tuning procedures remain unchanged. Expanded mathematical descriptions and the additional embedding robustness evaluation do not establish a revision to the core method.

E1.justification: Both versions use Crossmodal and Visual Genome, the same seven languages with five retained for LLaVA, and the same English/Japanese study populations. The untranslated-caption check reuses existing coverage and changes preprocessing and measurement.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparison methods remain unchanged. In particular, the English GIT/BLIP2 multimodel comparison is retained in v3 Table 14 and v4 Table 13, despite inconsistent BLIP naming in both versions' prose.

E3.justification: v4 Section 9.2 adds evaluation with multilingual Sentence-BERT on untranslated captions, changing the preprocessing and embedding instrument for this additional check. Existing fine-tuning splits of 1.8k training and 1.8k held-out images, caption compositions and SPICE evaluation remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v4 adds a robustness check asking whether greater multilingual embedding coverage persists without English translation (Section 9.2, Table 5). Existing multimodel comparisons, Visual Genome grounding, translation checks, cumulative scene-graph analysis and human study remain, including material moved into the supplement.

E5.justification: v4 adds p < 0.001 reporting for Table 5 but removes the ±0.60 accompanying v3's aggregate translation-quality rating of 4.68. Per-language summary statistics and Bonferroni-corrected comparisons remain. Neither version establishes an increase in repeated runs or seed counts.

E6.justification: v4 Table 5 adds untranslated-embedding results, including XM monolingual/multilingual averages of 0.280/0.340. Existing benchmark values remain; v4 Table 4 merely increases decimal precision. Revised prose contains mismatches: Section 2.2's 46.0% object increase matches XM averages rather than its stated English/French/Chinese comparison, and the introduction reports 0.23 for Japanese-trained evaluation on English captions versus Table 4's 0.212.

T1.justification: v4 Section 4 replaces v3's inconsistent loss-style fine-tuning inequality with a comparison using the defined higher-is-better score S and explicitly excludes identical language pairs. Most other added equations formalize existing operations; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: v3 presents its central contribution as evidence against homogeneous human perception, using language as a proxy for culture. v4 shifts the central claim to distributional semantic and expressive differences between captions across languages and their potential training value. This substantially narrows the scientific scope of the abstract, introduction and conclusion.

C2.justification: v4 removes the standalone cultural/historical and 'perception is not objective' implications and the explicit language-as-culture proxy limitation. It emphasizes distributional rather than categorical claims, newly interprets existing multimodel comparisons as countering 'different language modes', and attributes Vertex's smaller variation to standardized outputs. Recommendations concerning annotator-background collection and culturally conditioned applications are removed.

D1.justification: v4 identifies gpt-4-0613 and Vertex imagetext-001 and adds details about XM's shared instructions, English proficiency requirements and caption priming. Conversely, it omits v3's explicit Vertex caption totals and Visual Genome sample count. These are documentation changes without evidence that the retained experiments changed.

R1.justification: v4 substantially revises positioning around multilingual vision models, language biases and English-biased dataset filtering. It explicitly connects its findings to Nguyen et al.'s 2024 work on multilingual diversity improving vision-language representations. Numerous relevant works are added while several philosophical and annotator-diversity references supporting v3's broader framing are removed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and discussion are extensively rewritten. The language-level/model-level organization becomes separate sections on dataset variation, model variation and fine-tuning, with repeated Method/Results blocks. Related work, limitations and human-study findings move into the supplement, and acknowledgements are added.

P2.justification: v3's metric-oriented Tables 1, 2 and 4 are reorganized and transposed into v4's source-oriented Tables 1–2, and a new Table 5 is added. Figure 2 is reduced and relocated, Figure 1's caption changes, and supplementary text and displays are substantially regrouped. Existing figure graphics remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: Narrowing v3's broad cultural-perception argument to measured caption distributions improves alignment between evidence and conclusions. v4 also organizes the evidence more clearly and adds a useful untranslated-embedding check. These provide a limited net improvement despite mismatched numerical examples in the introduction and Section 2.2, and removal of the translation-rating dispersion.
